title: Walls, floors, cabinets: what the condo association insures, and what your own policy has to cover
seoTitle: Florida Condo Insurance: Association Policy vs. HO-6
description: Florida law splits a condo between the association's policy and the owner's HO-6. Here is who insures the floors, cabinets, water heater and more.
dek: Florida law draws a line through every condo unit. The building's policy covers one side. Your own policy has to cover the other. Here is where the line falls, in plain words.
facebook: Who insures your kitchen cabinets: you or the condo association? Florida law answers that, item by item. Here's where the line falls, the $2,000 your own policy must include, and what to check this week.
keywords: what does condo association insurance cover in Florida
who insures condo cabinets and floors Florida
is the condo association responsible for my water heater

body.text: Many condo owners assume the association's insurance covers "the building" and their own policy covers "my stuff." That is close, but Florida law is more exact than that. It names, item by item, which parts of a unit the association insures and which parts the owner is responsible for.

This is a plain-words guide to what the law says. It is not legal or insurance advice. Your own declaration (the condo's founding document) and your own policy matter too. For your unit, talk with your insurance agent, your manager or board, and if needed the association attorney.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Association policy: the property insurance the condo association buys for the building, paid for out of everyone's assessments. HO-6: the common name for a condo unit owner's policy, which mainly covers your belongings and your personal liability. Common elements: the parts of the condo everyone shares, like the roof, hallways and structure. Limited common elements: shared parts set aside for one unit or a few, like a balcony or an assigned parking space. Replacement cost: what it would cost to rebuild, not what the building would sell for.
What the association must insure

Section 718.111(11) of the 2026 Florida Statutes is the condo insurance law. It says every association must carry "adequate" property insurance, no matter what the declaration says. The replacement cost of the property must be figured at least once every 3 years.

For policies issued or renewed since January 1, 2009, the association's policy must cover the condo property as it was originally built, or replacements of like kind and quality. That includes the structure and the common elements. It also covers certain later additions to the common property made under the law's rules.
The association may also buy other coverage, such as flood insurance and liability coverage for its directors and officers.
What the association policy leaves out: your list

The same subsection lists items inside your unit, or in its limited common elements, that the association policy does not have to cover. The law says that property "and any insurance thereupon is the responsibility of the unit owner." The list is:

items: Your personal property: furniture, clothes, electronics and everything else you own.
Floor, wall and ceiling coverings: carpet, tile, wood floors, paint and wallpaper.
Window treatments: curtains, drapes, blinds and their hardware.

body.text: So in a typical unit, the walls themselves may be the association's job, but the paint, the flooring, the kitchen cabinets and the water heater are yours to insure. Your declaration can add details, so read it alongside the statute.
What your HO-6 has to include
Section 627.714 of the 2026 Florida Statutes sets rules for unit owner policies. Two matter most for everyday owners.

First, loss assessment coverage. If the association charges every owner a share of a covered loss to the common property, this part of your policy can help pay your share. Policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2010, must include at least $2,000 of this coverage. That is a floor, not a ceiling. Many agents offer higher limits, and the right amount is a question for your own agent.

Second, your policy is excess coverage. The law says it must state that it pays only beyond what any other policy covering the same property pays. In other words, the association policy goes first on the property it covers.
The state's Department of Financial Services (DFS) describes an HO-6 as a policy that "primarily covers the personal property and liability of the insured," with some coverage for the structure.
Who pays for repairs after damage

The law also says who handles rebuilding. After an insured event, the association must do the reconstruction work on the property it insures, and that cost is a common expense shared by all owners. Owners pay to rebuild the parts they are responsible for insuring, and the association can collect that cost as an assessment.

There is an exception owners should know. If the damage was caused by an owner, or by a family member, tenant, guest or other occupant, through intentional conduct, negligence, or breaking the condo's rules, that owner can be charged for repair costs that insurance does not cover. Associations can opt out of these default rules by a vote of a majority of the total voting interests, meaning more than half of all the votes in the condo, not just those present at a meeting. If yours did, a notice of the vote must be recorded.
What to do
If you own a unit:

items: Pull out your HO-6 and find the loss assessment limit. Ask your agent whether it fits the size of your building and its budget.
Make sure your policy covers your floors, cabinets, countertops, fixtures, appliances and water heater, not just your furniture.
Ask the manager for a summary of the association's current policy.
Read the insurance section of your declaration and check whether the association ever voted to opt out of the default rules.

body.text: If you serve on the board:

items: Check when the building's replacement cost was last determined. The law requires it at least once every 3 years.
Review the association's coverage with its insurance agent and the association attorney.
Send owners a short note explaining which items they must insure. Many owners do not know the list exists.
For questions the statute does not answer, ask the association attorney or DFS's consumer helpline at 1-877-693-5236.

faq.q: Does the condo association insurance cover my kitchen cabinets in Florida?
faq.a: Usually not. Section 718.111(11)(f) lists built-in cabinets and countertops among the items inside a unit that the association policy does not have to cover. They are the owner's responsibility to insure. Check your declaration too.

faq.q: Who insures the water heater in a Florida condo?
faq.a: Under section 718.111(11)(f), water heaters and water filters are on the list of items the association policy excludes, so insuring them is the unit owner's job.

faq.q: How much loss assessment coverage does a Florida condo owner need?
faq.a: Section 627.714 requires at least $2,000 of loss assessment coverage on unit owner policies issued or renewed since July 1, 2010. That is the minimum; your agent can explain higher limits.

faq.q: Does the condo association insurance cover my floors and walls?
faq.a: The association insures the building's structure as originally built. But floor, wall and ceiling coverings, like carpet, tile, wood floors and paint, are on the list the owner must insure.

faq.q: How often must a Florida condo update its insurance replacement cost?
faq.a: Section 718.111(11)(a) requires the replacement cost to be determined at least once every 3 years.
